Wandering Prince
Avatar the Last Airbender, Zuko SI
31
Commissioned by Tevod.
Suki yawned as she rose to meet the day. Looking around at the other girls sleeping in the barracks, she frowned as she noticed a bed empty that she wasn't expecting. Standing, she pulled on her robe in the cool morning air and checked the room where their guests were staying, to find it empty. A thrill of fear and doubt ran through her as, for a moment, she wondered if they hadn't been deceived.

Making her way outside, she found her missing sister fully dressed and leaning against the wall with her eyes closed. "Where are they?"

The other girl cracked open an eye tiredly and made an irritated sound. "Zuko got up earlier and dragged Toph off to the beach. Just tossed her onto his shoulder like a bag of rice. I don't think she ever actually woke up. After last night, not really all that surprised. You said not to leave them without an escort, so one of us had to go with them and someone needed to be awake to let you know. That's done." Pushing off the wall, she headed inside with a grumbled, "Wake me up when breakfast is ready, Suki."

Suki made her way back inside and got to work on breakfast and their meals for the rest of the day—leftover pig from the night before, some rice, and vegetables. Soon enough, the rest of the girls were up and sitting around the table in various states of undress, slowly eating and sipping at their tea as they worked through the process of waking up for the day. Taking in her exhausted looking sisters and their sluggish movements, bags under their eyes, and general cranky attitude, Suki scoffed.

"If you're going to let a little missed sleep get to you like this, I think we need to increase our training," Suki threatened.

There was a moment of collective silence as the other three girls at the table looked at each other. Even the usually snappy retorts were slow to come, and when they did they were missing their usual zing.

"It was after midnight before they stopped, Suki."

"And they woke me up before dawn so they could go train on the beach."

"Not even you're that enthusiastic about training."

"Normally, I'd love the idea of a guy with amazing stamina, you know? But…"

"Not when they're in the room next door and we have to listen to it."

"Who knew someone that small could be that loud?"

"I am uncomfortably chafed and my fingers are cramping."

"Same."

"I think I bruised something."

"Maybe we should tell them to be mindful of others?"

"And spoil the show?"

"That was the most exciting thing we've heard or done that didn't involve killing pirates in months. You can't."

"You know, while they're out, we could take this time to cut peep holes into the walls. For, uh, security."

"Ooh, good idea!"

"I'll get the saw—"

"Girls," Suki growled, glaring at the others as they began perking up at the prospect of doing something naughty. "Do not bring shame upon the legacy of the Kyoshi Warriors."

Another moment of silence, then…

"So don't get caught."

"We can do that."

"No! Don't do it at all—!" Suki protested, only to be cut off by one of the others.

"So you don't want us to cut you a peephole?"

Suki opened her mouth, then closed it with a click of teeth. After a moment, she looked away. "They'll be able to see a hole from inside, so make sure you plug them properly." Glaring at the others, she added, "And we're only adding them so we can make sure they're not doing anything they shouldn't, like sneaking off in the middle of the night!"

"Uh huh."

"Keep telling yourself that, Suki."

"You don't have to lie to us, you know."

"Ugh. Shut up, all of you. Hurry up and finish eating so we can get to work," Suki grumbled as she shoveled a bite of food into her mouth.

They hurried through the rest of the meal and quickly got ready for the day, before heading out. As they left the barracks, Suki considered for a moment before giving orders. "The three of you, head up to the lookout and scout. I'll head down to the beach. Meet us there."

The other girls gave their agreements and they split up. Suki took off at a light jog through the forest down towards the beach, allowing her mind to wander as her body moved purely by memory down the familiar path. Eventually, the beach came into sight and she hurried down it, finding the figures of Zuko, Toph, and her wayward sister all lined up along the shore.

As she drew closer, the sun peeked above the horizon to the east, framed by two of the mountains and casting a long, orange ray over the beach and water in front of her while leaving much of the rest of it in shadow. Water sparkled and sand gleamed white as they caught the first rays of sun, but that wasn't what stole Suki's breath and caused her to slow.

Zuko stood wearing nothing but a set of short clothes, facing away from her towards the water they were standing in, the sun catching his lightly tanned skin in a way that drew Suki's gaze. Her blue eyes roamed over his muscular body as he moved, stretching and moving in a slow kata, the movements making his muscles tighten in ways that made her mouth go dry, all of that moisture flooding south as another part of her turned perilously wet. Occasionally, the light caught a jagged streak of white scar tissue at his shoulder and a few along his ribs on the left side. When he turned enough that she could see his chest, she saw the remains of a scar the likes of which she'd never seen before over his heart.

Beside him, Toph had taken off her own robe and wore only her breast bindings and a set of similar short clothes on her bottom as she moved through a form of her own. And on the other side of Toph stood Suki's sister, likewise going through her own forms as part of their usual morning training routine, when they weren't out hunting pirates anyway.

Studying the two benders, Suki frowned as she noticed something seemed strange about the way Zuko moved. She had faced firebenders a time or two before—they'd had to run a few of them off the island when they came around wanting to start trouble in the past. She knew how they moved. The sharp, fast, direct and mostly straight line movements that would send balls of fire flying into their surroundings.

Some of his movements were exactly that, certainly—if performed at something like one quarter speed as he was obviously doing a muscle tension resistance exercise. But there were parts that were not what she was expecting. They were… circuitous. Moving not in lines, but in curves and arcs, or back and forth like the waves lapping at their feet.

"We'll be done with our warm-up in a few minutes and then we'll move on to sparring. You're welcome to join us, Suki."

"I'll think about it," the redhead murmured.

Toph scoffed. "Guess she's afraid to fight without all her friends backing her up. Well, I can't blame her. We're kind of awesome."

Suki's eyes shifted to her sister who didn't even turn to look before chiming in, "Oh no Suki, don't drag me into this. I'm going back home when I'm done here, so I can sleep for a few hours, since I had the last watch shift."

Frowning, Suki looked to Zuko and asked, "No firebending?"

"I haven't sparred with just swords in a while," he admitted. Looking to Toph, he asked, "You good?"

"Still figuring out sand," she grumbled. "Go ahead."

"Swords it is then. I'll do my firebending stuff after," Zuko agreed. Whatever form he was doing came to an end and he moved up the beach to their clothes. Picking up his pants, he shook them out and stepped into them, cinching them up and pulling on his belt with his sword. Still barefoot, he waved to Suki to follow and led her some distance away from the others.

Suki stopped long enough to set down her lunch and canteen and followed, stretching a bit to loosen up as she walked. When they were roughly a hundred yards from the others, Zuko stopped and turned around, sending Suki a smile. "Rules?"

Considering for a moment, Suki decided to stick with what she knew. "We'll go by points. First to five points or to force their opponent to surrender wins. If one of us can't continue they lose. A solid hit with the flat of the sword is a point. Disarming your opponent earns you two points. Anything worse than a nick to draw blood costs two points."

The man across from her considered for a moment before nodding, a smile on his face. "Alright. I'll add the condition that if I do any bending, I lose automatically."

"Okay," Suki agreed.

With that, she settled into a wider stance and drew her sword, holding it defensively as she waited. Zuko's own sword slid smoothly from its sheath and he slowly began to circle her, forcing Suki to move to keep them even. The man's face shifted from its lighthearted expression to dead serious and the change was so stark that a thrill of fear ran through Suki and settled in her gut as her heart hammered in her chest, and she gripped her katana just a bit tighter.

She wondered what he was doing, since he wasn't pushing her towards the water to limit her movement options—instead, he was backing himself towards the water. That's when the sword held in his grip shifted and Suki winced as a flash of light off the blade blinded her, reflected from the sunrise behind her. She moved instinctively to the side, blinking spots out of her vision as she heard Zuko's footsteps rushing her. In no condition to meet him head on, she sprung backwards, trying to put more space between them.

That was when beachgrass caught her sandal and Suki tripped, falling back on her ass with a thump in the sand. Zuko was on top of her in the next moment, knocking her sword out of her hand and tapping the side of her face with the flat of the blade.

"That two or three?" the jerk asked, grinning down at her. His smug look wasn't the first thing she wanted to see when her vision cleared, but there it was. Smug and damn handsome—

Suki sighed. "Three."

Shifting his sword to his other hand, Zuko offered her a hand up. Suki eyed it for just a moment before accepting the offered hand. He hauled her to her feet like she weighed nothing. Which, as much as Suki and the girls would deny it, wasn't actually true. Muscle was heavy and the girls were all very fit, even if they weren't particularly bulky. She knew none of them were what she would call light.

Strong, she thought, before shaking her head and stooping to pick up her sword. Focus, Suki!

They separated and, as soon as they reset, Suki launched herself at him, whipping her katana forward in a quick thrust, which transitioned into a slash towards his arm when Zuko moved out of the way. His sword came up and parried her own, easily forcing it aside as he closed the distance between them, swinging for her midsection. Suki's sword was out of position to do anything about it, so she was forced to give ground for the moment.

His sword whooshed by her abdomen, close enough that she felt the tug of the tip against her armor. But with the momentum of his swing working against him and his own sword out of position, Suki retaliated with a quick slash that thumped against Zuko's arm.

The man chuckled, nodding to her as he backed away. They reset and Suki went for him again, coming in with a high overhead strike to take him at the shoulder or force him to block, and then she would kick then go in for a sweep and disarm—

Something clicked and Suki blinked as Zuko stepped into her swing, his sword coming up in his left hand to catch and lock her blade, his one arm strong enough to hold against both of hers—maybe not for long, but long enough, as he brought the sword in his right hand around and thumped her firmly in the side.

Suki frowned as she stepped back, glaring at the man who gave the twin swords in his hands a flourish. "Well if that's how you want to play," Suki grumbled. Reaching behind herself, she grabbed her collapsible shield and flicked it open, taking up a stance more suited for fighting defensively.

"Oh, neat. Is that spring loaded?" Zuko asked, nodding at the shield.

"Beat me and I'll tell you," Suki taunted.

The man nodded and dashed at her. Suki braced herself and caught the first blow on her shield. Her katana flashed out in a jab, but Zuko wasn't there. He hit her with the full weight of his body as he leapt, slamming into the shield as he dropped the sword he'd hit her with, planted his hand on the shield, and flipped over her.

Suki allowed herself to fall backwards into the sand, narrowly missing getting hit with a swing that would have caught her in the head. She rolled back onto her knees in time to see Zuko land and slip on the sand—putting him off balance for a moment. A moment was all she needed as Suki launched herself forward and smashed into him with her shield, knocking his sword away and sending them to the ground.

Everything became a chaotic tumble after that as they rolled in the sand, and Suki found her katana wrenched from her hand and thrown away. She punched and kneed, and got a punch to the chest and a knee to the gut herself in return as the sword fight devolved into an attempt to grapple each other.

Finally, Suki's arm was wrenched up behind her back and her body pressed face first into the ground, Zuko's weight pinning her there. She tried to buck him off, but the man didn't go anywhere. Turning her head, Suki snorted out a nose full of sand and panted, eyeing the man on top of her as he looked down on her.

His body was flush against her own, hot and heavy as he breathed deeply to catch his breath. She raised her hips experimentally—just trying to dislodge him—and felt something firm brush against her rear end. She found herself thankful for her makeup as she felt herself blushing as she realized just what it was pressing between her cheeks.

Finally, her mouth opened and ran off ahead of her brain, voicing the thoughts that would definitely get her in trouble one day. "Is that a sword in your pants or are you just happy to see me?"

Argh! What was I thinking?! You're supposed to set an example for the others, not an example for how not to act!

"Why can't it be both?" the man grinned down at her.

For just a moment, Suki was rendered speechless. Narrowing her eyes, she growled, "Will you get off me?"

"Sure, but before I do… What was that score again?"

Suki thought back over the fight and frowned, realizing she had lost count. Annoyed, she admitted, "I don't remember."

Nodding, Zuko asked, "In that case, getting the pin has to count for a win, right?"

Suki blew out an irritated breath. As much as it pained her to admit, he was right. He had her dead to rights and she couldn't do anything to get him off of her at the moment. "Fine."

"Great." Zuko let go of her hand and pushed himself up. Suki rolled over and accepted the hand up he offered, then started retrieving her equipment. "So, go again?"

"If she won't, we'll definitely take a turn!"

"I wouldn't mind getting some practice in."

"Screw the sword practice, let's skip straight to the grappling!"

"We should take our clothes off first so they don't get dirty."

"I will bury you all up to your necks," Toph grumbled as Suki dusted herself off with as much dignity as she could manage, given the peanut gallery of her girls running their mouths.

"Sorry girls," Zuko sent them a smile, "but I promised Toph she's the only one I'll be doing any naked wrestling with any time soon."

"Aww!"

"That sucks."

"Can we watch?"

"We can score it."

"Ugh," Suki groaned. "Girls! Rein it in!"

"Well, if that's what you're into Suki…"

"I'm sure we can find a saddle and tack somewhere on the island."

"Maybe a collar and leash instead?"

"No, it's obviously the crop and spurs she's interested in."

"I am going to smother you in your sleep," Suki hissed, glaring at the others as they teased her.

"Anyway," Zuko laughed, catching the robe top Toph threw at him and shaking out the sand, before starting to pull it on. "How about we survey the island and get to work? We've got a few days to prepare before we set out looking for the pirates. In the meantime, Toph can handle building new structures if you don't mind them being made of stone, and if you've got any wounded, you can bring them to me."

"Surveying would take all day," Suki shook her head. "We can just take you to where the worst of it is. And we've already taken care of first aid. The remaining injured need a healer or time."

Toph and Zuko exchanged a look at that and something seemed to pass between them, before the girl shrugged. Turning back to Suki, Zuko pulled a knife from his belt. "No, I meant bring them to me for healing."

"What? You studied medicine or something?" Suki asked, and the man shook his head as he stepped closer. "Then what—what are you doing?! Stop!"

Suki grabbed the knife out of Zuko's hand as he drew a deep cut in the top of his arm with a look of pain. Grabbing the arm, she looked at the wound—at least four inches long and down to the bone. "This is going to need stitches! Why did you do that? Are you stupid?!"

"Just watch," Zuko murmured, before holding up his free hand. The hand lit with green fire and Suki took a step back, suddenly feeling sick to her stomach as a premonition came over her. She could almost smell the burning flesh already and her stomach churned—

The other girls watched in silence as he ran the fire over his arm. Contrary to their expectations, his arm didn't burn—it didn't so much as blister. Instead, the skin knitted together neatly, leaving only blood behind. Taking out a canteen of his own, Zuko washed the arm off with water, leaving behind unblemished, tan skin. Not even a scar remained.

"No way."

"How did you…?"

"It's got to be a trick, right?"

"Can't be. You saw it. There was blood everywhere."

"What was that?" Suki asked, looking between Zuko and Toph.

The man chuckled. "I can heal. Cuts, bruises, stab wounds, infection, I can even regrow missing limbs."

"Or cure the blind," Toph murmured, a smile on her face as she looked at Zuko that told Suki there was a story there.

"That too," Zuko nodded, gesturing for them to follow as he began walking up the beach, towards the ship they had arrived on. "It's not great for internal stuff or for anything that requires a whole lot of precision, at least not as good as waterbending, but it does work."

"That's amazing!"

"Suki, we should go let the other villages know."

"Gather everyone in one location so he can do them all at once."

"I guess I can put off going to bed to help out with this."

Suki considered Zuko in silence for a few moments as the girls chattered, before asking, "What's it going to cost?"

Zuko sent her a knowing look. It was Toph who answered, however, "A little food and some supplies. Coal if you've got it, to offset what we're going to use hunting down the pirates. And you'll let us stay here for a while after we get finished."

Suki glanced at the other girls, who all nodded. Finally, she said, "We'll ask Oyaji and see what he says."

"And that is…?" Zuko asked, hopping up onto the metal boat he and Toph had arrived in as the girls followed.

"The leader of the largest village on the island," Suki answered as she followed the others up, watching as Zuko lit the coal furnace and added some more fuel, before joining Toph on top of the small ship. "What are you doing?"

The pair unlatched a long tube, exposing a large roll of canvas or something similar that reminded Suki of a sail and began fitting a circular opening in it over a pipe coming from the top of the ship. "Just wait. Trust me, you're gonna love this," Toph sent them a grin as they worked.

Slowly, Suki watched as the sail? began to expand? Fill up? It rose and swelled as it filled with what must be hot air coming directly from the engine.

What kind of sail needs hot air?

In just a few minutes, the whole thing had unfurled above the ship, pulling tight against the ropes holding it in place. Then, a moment later, the ship wobbled underfoot. Suki and the girls nearly lost their balance as it slowly lifted up out of the sand, their eyes going wide as they looked at each other, while Zuko and Toph laughed and jumped down from the roof, taking their places at the back of the ship where the controls were. Zuko pushed a lever forward and their rise accelerated, and Suki widened her stance to keep from falling.

The other girls rushed to the sides of the ship and grabbed onto the edge or the ropes holding the sail above them up as they looked out over the island as they quickly began to rise. Suki made her way to the front, a quiet gasp escaping her as something from the rear of the ship hummed loudly and the ship began moving forward, turning to the right—to starboard—and pulling out over the water, before adjusting course to port as it began to follow the shoreline, putting the island below them and on their left.

Her heart hammered in her chest and Suki wasn't sure if it was fear, excitement, or both. They made her short of breath as they steadily rose above even the tallest mountains on Kyoshi Island. Looking out over the island, she realized she could see all of the little villages scattered across the land, including their own. Not only that, but they could see for miles and miles out to sea in every direction as they cleared the level of the mountains.

This is how they're going to hunt the pirates. This… sky ship is faster than any boat, even the ones in the Fire Navy. They don't have to go around any obstacle when they can go over. Waves aren't an issue. And it seems the higher we go, the further the horizon becomes, so they would be able to spot a pirate ship miles off.

A thought occurred and Suki swallowed on a suddenly dry throat.

If Zuko, the prince of the Fire Nation, is here in a ship that can fly, then the Fire Nation already has this capability. The war is over. They've won. There is nothing we can realistically do from the ground if they decide to launch an attack from so high up that we can't retaliate with bows, earth, or water. All they would have to do is just… fly over and drop stones on whatever they wanted. Send men down into key areas, completely bypassing defenses.

…No. No, if they had something like this, they'd do what the Fire Nation always does. Mass produce it. We would have already seen them. Maybe he invented it himself. In that case… it can't get back to the Fire Nation or we're all dead.

Biting her lip, Suki shook her head. No, hang on. Let's not go off half drawn. I'll ask first and see what he says.

Turning away from the prow of the ship, she silently made her way back, where Zuko and Toph were sitting on a bench at the back of the ship, the Earth Kingdom girl leaning against Zuko and sighing happily as he rubbed his fingers gently over her eyes—a light green flame radiating from under them. "That feels so good~," Toph moaned quietly.

Suki paused, glancing between the two. Zuko looked up and sent her a smile. "Eye strain. She's still not quite used to going without the blindfold."

For just a moment, Suki almost asked about the ship. Instead, she took a moment to reassess as she watched the earthbender sitting practically in Zuko's lap relax under his ministrations. Changing her mind, she asked, "Blindfold?"

"Yeah. Toph has been blind since birth," Zuko explained absently, watching the shorter girl's face as he worked. "When Yue and I arrived in Gaoling, we met her after catching her fighting in an underground arena."

"I broke his leg," Toph chirped, sounding entirely too happy about that fact to Suki's ears.

Zuko rolled his eyes. "Long story short, she decided to leave Gaoling with us after she had a disagreement with her parents over the future of their company and her role in it. I fixed her eyes and she's been stuck to my side ever since."

Toph snorted quietly, smacking Zuko in the side, then reaching up and gently pushing his hand down from her eyes. Those pretty, jade green eyes opened and turned to Suki. "He's downplaying it. My parents tried every doctor, healer, medicine man, shaman, and snake oil salesman they could pay to look at me, and blindly trusted every one who showed up on their doorstep claiming to have a cure. All of them said the same thing. They all started off with high hopes that they could do something. Then they'd try whatever treatments, potions, salves, poultices, antidotes, or other crap they brought along. And when it all failed, they'd try to bilk my parents for money anyway. Some even claimed it wouldn't work on the first time but if they would just keep buying and using their swill for a few years it was bound to work. Eventually, they wised up."

"Can't blame your parents for being desperate and wanting to help," Zuko told her, reaching up to pet Toph's head.

The girl rolled her eyes. "No, but I can blame them for falling for every scam." Taking a breath, she shook her head. "Anyway. Then, this jerk and Yue showed up one day. They were practicing near my house when I was heading back. Of course, I thought it was some firebender attacking a waterbender…"

Suki winced, letting out a quiet groan as Toph chuckled. "At least I'm not the only one to make that mistake."

"Doubt you'll be the last, either," Zuko shrugged.

"So I attacked. And like I said, I broke his leg. An asshole can't run away if you break his legs, right?" Toph grinned, and Suki nodded as she laughed quietly. "They explained what was going on and Zuko healed his own leg. I couldn't see with my eyes at the time, but I can kind of see with earthbending through the ground, so I could tell what he'd done but not the how. We hung out for a while after that, had some fun, and eventually they decided it was time to leave. I got into an argument with my parents and decided to run away with them. By that point, I knew Zuko could heal people too, and better in some ways than Yue. So when we stopped for the night, I asked why he hadn't offered to try, since literally everyone else had. He said he didn't even know if it would work and didn't want to get my hopes up in case it didn't."

"But it did," Suki murmured, and Toph nodded.

"Oh yeah. It worked. Needed a blindfold though, because I'd never seen before, and the sun is bright. You know how it stings when you walk from a dark room into the sun? It's like that, but if you've lived your entire life in a cave. I've gotten way better since then. But my eyes still get tired or achy after a while sometimes."

Suki nodded. "I see."

"What were you going to ask?" Blinking, she looked over to Zuko, sending her a curious look. "You looked like you had something you wanted to ask when you came back here."

Crossing her arms, Suki looked down at the Earth Kingdom girl completely relaxed and happy right where she was, pressed up against the Fire Nation man's side. Then, there was the fact that they apparently traveled with another woman, from the Water Tribe—a healer and waterbender from what she'd gathered.

The jaded part of Suki wanted to believe that what she was seeing couldn't be real. That it had to be some kind of trick. There was no way the son of Fire Lord Ozai, a man renown for his petty cruelty even outside of the Fire Nation, could be so different from what she expected.

And yet, the hopeful romantic in her heart wanted to believe what her eyes were telling her. That maybe, just maybe, there was hope for the future. For a resolution to the Hundred Year War that didn't end in everyone subjugated under Fire Nation rule.

In the end, I suppose it comes down to trust. Someone must be willing to bend, to take the leap of faith first.

Finally, Suki shook her head. "Nothing important. Now, when do we set off after the pirates?"

#4,048
Wandering Prince
Avatar the Last Airbender, Zuko SI
32
Commissioned by Tevod.
Toph breathed in slowly as she sat, eyes closed, listening to the ocean waves rolling in against the beach as the sun set. Feeling the back and forth tugging and rolling motion against the sand of the beach, the sand stretching below the water. Everything was less clear than if she had been watching through dirt, and even less than if it had been stone, but after a while of practicing this she had begun to realize that it really was just like the difference between stone and dirt—it was all rock, all earth, just in smaller pieces. And while the sand may be loose and grainy, it was packed even more tightly than normal forest dirt.

It just took some getting used to, to see through it. Zuko had actually been a bigger help with that than he'd known—or than she was going to tell him.

What Toph sensed through the ground was vibrations. Waves, as he described it—much like the ones rolling over the beach, but faster, smaller, and each with their own frequency in how often they repeated or distance between waves and amplitude, the height or strength of the wave. Sound was also just a wave, and it had a set speed that it traveled through everything—faster through more dense material, slower through looser material, and not at all in the absence of anything to travel through.

He had put words to something she already knew from experience but hadn't actually put much thought into. Toph knew vibrations and sounds moved faster or slower depending on what she was sensing them through. She would often feel thunder through the ground long before she heard it far in the distance with her ears as it traveled through the air.

How fast those vibrations moved through something depended on what that thing was, which determined how well she would detect things with earthbending. Sand? Sand was made of a bunch of different stuff. What Zuko called an aggregate. So sound wasn't entirely consistent through it, but it was slightly better than water and way better than air for sensing—which was good enough for Toph.

Bats and bat-critters existed. As did dolphins and dolphin-critters. And those animals all used something Zuko called echolocation—what he had called how she saw through rock, when she'd first explained it. Well, no, she remembered what he called what she did as tremorsense, but he said it was similar to echolocation—the only difference being that tremorsense was passive, while echolocation was active, meaning that those animals made their own sounds to see by, instead of relying on other things making sound for them. And how they got a stable picture was by making sound constantly.

So Toph's thought was simple… if dolphins could see through water and bats could see through air, then seeing through sand should be entirely possible. All she had to do was make sound—preferably something people couldn't actually hear and which wouldn't upset every animal in a mile radius.

That was why she was sitting on the beach as the tide came in, listening and feeling how the constant low roar of it spread through the sand and lit up everything within and on the sand to her senses. Why she had been practicing finding and creating different pitches of sound by vibrating the ground beneath her and seeing what traveled best, and what provided the most clarity to her senses.

Reaching into the earth below her, Toph began vibrating the sand, creating a low vibration that rang in her bones and carried to her ears in an annoying way that felt like it was shaking her skull from the inside. Around her, she felt the sand ripple and move outwards, splashing up into the air in a cloud of dust. The beach lit up to her senses as she felt the vibrations roll around and off of everything on the surface and buried for hundreds of feet down. She adjusted the output, lowering the pitch until it passed outside the range her ears could hear.

It takes more time for the vibrations to reach anything and come back so I can sense it, but with it working constantly, even on sand there are no blind spots and it doesn't seem like there's really a delay in between something moving on the surface and me seeing it. At least, not enough of one to affect a fight.

Standing, eyes still closed, Toph focused on the sand below her that she could now sense properly—down to the individual grains. Moving into a basic earthbending kata, she frowned when the stuff still didn't respond the way she wanted and the best she could really do was create geysers or launch balls of sand that fell apart yards away from where she launched them.

She came to a stop and considered the problem. Obviously, she was doing something wrong.

Glancing back at the shore and the waves rolling over it, Toph hummed. "Maybe I should try that earth-as-water thing," she mused quietly, before shrugging.

With the back and forth motion of the waves moving as a constant background guide, Toph began to experiment, changing the way she moved her chi within herself and the earth below. In and out, back and forth, over and over. Step forward, her arms thrust forward. Pull back, draw her arms back. Forward again, slowly advancing up the beach one step forward half a step back at a time.

It was slow going at first, but eventually, she felt it begin to change as she found a rhythm that worked. Then, on the next draw inwards, sand hissed as it rushed around her feet, over her ankles, piling up behind her. She stepped forward, out of the stand, and the piled up mass rushed forward, carrying her with it and causing her to stumble and fall on her face.

Laughing, Toph stood up and dusted herself off, before trying again. Keeping her eyes open this time, she watched as she drew sand in towards herself and sent it rushing back out across the beach in a wave. From there, it was just a matter of figuring out what she could do.

It was as she created a small wave beneath herself and solidified the sand beneath her feet into something closer to sandstone and sent herself surfing up and down the beach fast enough to make her eyes water that everything just seemed to click into place in her mind and she got it. It wasn't that sand didn't behave like stone—it did. No, it just behaved like an entire avalanche of tiny little boulders falling all over each other at the same time. And because there were so many of them, they were so tiny and so light, and they bounced off of each other and everything around them like they did that they also moved like water.

But that didn't mean that she couldn't reshape them—either individually or the whole mass. It didn't mean she couldn't make them solid—she just had to force them to come together properly. She just had to change the way she was thinking about it. She couldn't just do big shoves and hits the way she could with normal rock, because all that would get her was big jets of sand blasting whichever way she pointed. Most of the aggregate that made up the whole of sand—or at least, the sand on this beach—was rounded and smoothed out by water, wind, and time with only a bit of it more roughly shaped. That was why it had trouble holding together.

So, what if I change how it's shaped and start merging pieces?

Sitting down near the water again, she cupped a handful of sand and focused on it. Willing it to change shape the way she shaped stone to make structures. To merge together, bit by bit, into the shape she wanted.

Slowly, she felt the change start—first one piece, then a few, then hundreds at a time, then thousands. Until eventually, the whole of the mass of sand in her hand flowed together. First, it became more like the consistency of mud, then clay, until it hardened to a white stone as solid as anything she had ever created before. Picking up more sand, she did it again—faster this time. Grinning, she reached into the ground below her and sand flowed, solidifying as it rose beneath her into a sphere larger than she was tall in just a few seconds.

Grinning like a loon, she reached into the stone in her hand that she'd created and broke it down, reversing the process—except with the intention of making every grain shaped more like tiny grains of rice… very sharp grains of rice. That turned out to be a very bad idea when, the moment she went to move it off of her hand, it shredded her palm.

Toph yelped, crushing the sharp sand back into a rock and pulling out all of the pieces that had embedded themselves into her hand. "Shit," she winced, pulling her belt off and wrapping her hand up.

Right. Don't play with sharp sand myself. But uh… definitely using that on someone. I need to see what else I can do with it.
"…And that's when Hei Bai got him. At least, we think that's what happened. He screamed. The spirit roared. When we got there, there was nothing but a panda-shaped spirit and a few tracks."

Suki winced, sucking in a breath. "Right. Don't make the spirits angry," she murmured.

We stepped out onto the beach from the path and I spotted Toph down by the shore. As we started that way, I continued, "Generally a good idea, yeah. Though sometimes, that's not really something you can avoid."

Suki nodded once. "Dealing with spirits is one of the duties of the Avatar."

I shook my head. "No, being the bridge between the spiritual and the physical realms is the Avatar's most important duty. Everything else should come after. Personally, I don't believe they should get involved in earthly politics at all."

"The Fire Nation would say that."

Rolling my eyes, I sent Suki an amused look. "Yes. Yes, I would. Do you know why?"

"Your people killed all of the airbenders, trying to break the Avatar cycle," she sent me a reproachful look.

"People in glass houses shouldn't throw stones."

Frowning, the redhead asked, "What's that supposed to mean?"

Raising an eyebrow, I asked, "Do you really want to hear how people outside of Kyoshi Island and the Earth Kingdom remember Avatar Kyoshi, and why that is?" When the girl looked away, I nodded. "Instead of blaming each other for the sins of our fathers, we should be working to make sure we don't leave any behind ourselves. Otherwise, the entire cycle is going to continue as it has historically with one nation blaming another for some slight, going to war with what they believe to be just cause, only for that nation to then wage war in the next generation and maybe decide to attack someone else for not helping them in their time of need or whatever reason they can convince their people of that it's worth it."

Suki thought on that for a few moments as we crossed the beach, before asking, "Fine. What does the Avatar not getting involved have to do with it?"

"The Avatar getting involved only makes things worse. Any conflict becomes larger in scale when the Avatar takes the field. More people die. Landscapes get rearranged. Nations change leaders. Worse, the Avatar taking a side can give the entire world reason to believe they're right, even when they're in the wrong. Think about it, Suki. What if Avatar Roku had decided to side with Sozin, his former best friend and brother in all but blood? He had every reason to. I think we both know what would've happened."

Suki went quiet for a moment, before murmuring, "The war would have been over long ago and we'd all be living under Fire Nation rule."

"Exactly. That's why I believe the Avatar should remain uninvolved, unless it gets to the point where they're the absolute last resort, or something so awful is happening that something needs to be done immediately. If Roku hadn't died, then the attempted genocide of the Air Nomads would have been plenty reason for him to step in and start sinking ships. Maybe bump Sozin off the throne and make sure that whoever took it next understood that killing off an entire group of benders to try to break the Avatar cycle is bad for everyone. But the four nations going to war for whatever reason? The Avatar should stay out of it, except to make sure that the war doesn't disturb the spirits. It's none of his business if the Earth Kingdom wants to expand their territory, or the Water Tribes are killing each other. The only time it would be is if, again, we're talking about wiping out another group entirely, or they made the mistake of attacking the Avatar's family."

"I don't like it."

I nodded. "Yeah. You're not supposed to."

"What?" she sent me a confused look.

Laughing, I explained, "That's the nature of compromise. Both sides want something. Neither gets what they want, or only get some of what they want, or they get what they want at a price. But either way, neither side is entirely happy about the result because not everything went the way they wanted. Otherwise, it wouldn't be compromise, but a mutually beneficial arrangement."

Suki glared at me. "Then you may as well ban coal powered ships and whatever else the Fire Nation have that the rest of us don't, because those things change the balance of power and can make wars worse."

"Concentration of power," I countered. "Ships cost money, materials, and man hours to build. A single ship—no, even a fleet of flying ships like mine can't do as much damage as quickly as the Avatar, and with so few people able to counter them. No, if you let the Avatar get involved in politics, you may as well just drop any pretense that nations have sovereignty—because at that point, rulers would only rule and nations would only act as long as the Avatar allowed. You may as well rename them from Avatar to Immortal God Emperor."

The girl opened her mouth to argue, only to pause, then slowly close it with a click as she frowned. Toph looked up as we approached and grinned, and Suki and I put the discussion on hold. "Hey guys. Zuko! Look what I can do!"

I raised an eyebrow as she narrowed her eyes and sand rose below us into what looked to my eyes like a perfect reconstruction of Gaoling, before shifting to Omashu, then Kyoshi Island. "Wow. That's some fine detail," I murmured, crouching down to study the buildings making up the island's villages. Frowning, I pointed and asked, "Wait, those are people. And they're moving."

"Heh heh! Yeah!" Toph nodded, squatting across from me and giving me a view of her muscular thighs and the pair of my boxers she had stolen for herself.

"Wait," Suki murmured, tilting her head to the side as she studied everyone moving about on the island. "You can sense everyone on the island from here?" she asked, and Toph nodded again. "How?"

"Echolocation," I answered immediately, and Toph pouted, sticking her tongue out at me.

"Yeah. I make a sound here, it hits something across the island, and comes back."

"How did you get around the limits with sand?" I asked. "If you can see through it at all, your range should be crap."

"Oh, it is," Toph nodded. "But!"

As she reached down to the sand, I noticed that one of her hands was wrapped in her belt. Taking it in my own, I unwrapped it and winced, before coating her hand in green fire. "Toph, what the hell? You should have said something."

"That looks nasty," Suki murmured, studying the other girl's hand as it quickly healed. "What did you do to it?"

The shorter girl shrugged. "No point whining about it when I did it to myself. Besides," she grinned at me, "I knew you'd fix it for me. Anyway! Watch!"

Holding up her fistful of sand, she squeezed her hand, before opening it and showing us a sand-colored rock. I cottoned on immediately. "You can meld sand into rock."

"Yuuup! That's how I hurt my hand. I made sharp sand and it uh, it just shredded everything. Didn't even try to do it."

"Uh huh," I murmured. "So the island?"

"Oh, I turned the sand below us into a big plate of rock. The sand only goes down a few feet now, and I made a pillar of stone up to me," she thumped one foot against the ground and it clacked beneath her as her stone sandal came into contact with the stone below. "I'm vibrating the whole thing so it's actually picking up a lot further than just the island, but there's not really anything interesting on the sea floor."

Chuckling, I stood and pulled her up, and into a hug. Toph made a surprised sound, but quickly returned the hug. "Have I told you you're awesome lately?"

"No."

"Well, you're awesome," I chuckled, kissing the top of her head and letting her go.

When she stepped back, the usually rambunctious tomboy was blushing. Looking away, she reached up and punched me in the arm hard enough to bruise later. Grinning, she nodded, "I know."

Nodding back towards the interior of the island, I started walking towards Suki's village and the girls followed. That is, until the sand below us rose up and solidified at the top, and we began rushing along the beach with a hiss of sand. Toph grinned as she reached out and took my hand. "Very nice," I laughed.

"Can't really do it on the trail back, unless I turn the whole path into rock or sand first," Toph admitted.

Suki shook her head. "Please don't. We don't want an easy trail straight from the beach to our home for just anyone to follow."

"Sure," Toph agreed as the swell of sand let us off into beachgrass. "So, when are we leaving to go after the pirates?"

"In a day or two. As soon as we get those supplies. I spent all day talking to Oyaji while you were busy. So, the old guy's basically the closest thing Kyoshi Island has to an official leader." Toph nodded at that and I continued, "He agreed. As long as we don't cause problems, we're allowed to stay. He even agreed to let us build ourselves a place to stay while we're here, so we're not imposing on Suki and the girls."

"It's not an imposition," Suki was quick to deny, but Toph snorted quietly.

"She means they don't want to have to cut new peep holes into whatever place I build for us," the gremlin leered up at Suki, who turned a glare on her. "But hey, good news is, if we've got our own place, you can all sleep soundly. No more rubbing yourselves raw at night."

Suki made an annoyed sound and looked away. "I have no idea what you're talking about. If we've been watching you, it's only to ensure the safety of the village."

"Uh huh. Suuure," Toph teased.

"Anyway," I sighed, reaching out and smacking Toph lightly on the back of the head. "Good work on the reconstruction and those walls."

"Thanks," she grinned, eating up the praise. "Wasn't hard. We got everything done before lunch."

"So," I sent Toph a curious look. "Tell me about this sharp sand stuff."

"Easier if I show you. I played around with the stuff a bit and it's kind of wild," she shook her head. Stomping her foot, a rock jutted out from the ground ahead, before dissolving into much darker colored sand. A thin tentacle of sand whipped towards a tree on the side of the path, wrapping around a limb overhead. It squeezed and moved, circling the limb as dust rained down. A moment later, the limb fell to the ground off to the side of the path. She whipped the tentacle out again, slashing the tree's trunk and leaving behind a deep, ragged gash that I fixed with green fire to avoid complaints about the destruction. Finally, the tentacle whipped out again and the leading edge narrowed and solidified, before thumping into another limb above and cutting straight through it.

"Okay. That's nasty," I murmured and Suki nodded.

"Remind me not to get on her bad side," the redhead mused as she picked up both limbs and looked them over. "Jagged cut on the first. It looks like something chewed through it. The second is clean, like a sword stroke."

I nodded. "Yeah, the first reminded me of a chainsaw."

"That's not all. Hold one of those out," Toph instructed, and Suki did as she asked. Narrowing her eyes, the end of the tentacle narrowed down and grew pointed, before stabbing forward and punching through the limb. There was a crack and the end of the limb exploded as the sand bulged and writhed, breaking it apart. Suki dropped the limb and stepped back, wincing as Toph laughed. "I was wrong before. Sand is awesome! But uh, if Yue got over her squeamishness, she could really do some nasty stuff."

"Oh yeah," I nodded. "You have no idea. Waterbending is one of the most underrated types of bending. But it looks like you figured out how to do earth as water?"

"Still working things out," Toph admitted. "But I've got ideas! I haven't been this excited about bending since figuring out metalbending." She paused, then gasped quietly. "Oh! Oh! This, but with metal! Zuko! We need to go to town! I need iron!"

"There's a small forge in our village," Suki supplied with a grin. "I'm sure they'd be happy to sell you some."

"What are you planning to do with it?" I asked, and Toph gave a malicious little giggle.

"Make iron sand."

"So iron filings," I supplied, and she nodded. "Nasty. I imagine it'll be easier to work with if you don't have to break it down every time you want to use it. So you'll need to keep it in something, because I don't want that stuff getting out and accidentally getting into our eyes, or our lungs."

Toph winced. "Yeah, that'd suck." Humming, she said, "And you did say I should carry a weapon. I can make normal sand take basically any shape I want, it's faster to work with than stone, and if I need to I can just turn it into stone…"

Another rock jumped from the ground and Toph caught it, reshaping it in her hands—turning it into sand as she reshaped and solidified it into a gourd shape, no different from what I'd seen more than one person walking around keeping their sake in. More rock poured from the ground, turning into sand and spinning together into a shape like a rope around the gourd as she hung it from the bloody belt around her waist. "There. That should be enough to make a good handle, and big enough inside to hold enough iron filings to make a decent hammer or something."

Considering the girl, I said, "Let me tell you about the flanged mace…"
"Are you sure this is going to work?" Toph asked as she and Suki eyed the set of metal water barrels I'd installed on the ship, and the hoses looped beside the rear two, attached to a pair of pumps I'd had some help building from Toph. On the top of each pair was copper tubing wound in a spiral leading from the rear tanks to the front tanks—with the spiral elevated slightly on the back end and lower at the front end to ensure proper water flow.

"It's simple science," I explained. "Without Yue, we need a way to make our own clean, fresh water. This is it."

"How does it work?" Suki asked, as Toph moved back to check the coal and make sure that was topped off. Inside, I could hear the other Kyoshi girls stowing their gear and setting up their hammocks from the loops I'd welded to the cabin's ceiling.

"We pump in salt water into the rear tanks using the pumps we made, then detach the hoses and seal the tanks. I heat the heating elements inside them with firebending and bring it up to boiling," I tapped a thermometer attached to the top of the tank I was standing beside. Unfortunately, I had no convenient way of properly measuring in Fahrenheit, so I'd done the next best thing of using Celsius—because as much as I hated it, the boiling point of water was a known element and setting that at one hundred was just more convenient at the moment.

"Salt water boils and becomes steam, but leaves the salt behind because the melting point of salt is way higher than the boiling point of water. Steam takes the path of least resistance into the copper pipe. Heat radiates outwards and it cools, and condenses back into water. Simple gravity flow means it flows into the fresh water tank and fills that. We lined the inside of those tanks with copper for a reason—to kill anything nasty that we can't see and prevent the water from spoiling. So, we should be good for drinking water. More copper pipes are connected to the spigot here and leads to the cabin inside, where I installed another pump, a coil around a bar of iron I can use as a heating element, a bath tub, and a small sink. If Toph turns the pump and I heat the water, we can have hot baths just big enough for two at a time, or use the sink. The drain on the bottom leads to the rear of the ship and has a shutoff valve both in the drain itself and outside to keep us from taking on water."

I'd have preferred making a shower, but that would require constant pumping and heating, as opposed to doing it once and soaking. And as thirsty as the Kyoshi girls acted, I sincerely doubted that they wanted me watching them shower just to provide hot water.

That, and Toph had suggested the idea of kicking the girls out of the cabin so we could bathe together and I liked the idea enough to go along with it.

"How are our supplies?" I asked, and Suki glanced towards the cabin, where the Kyoshi girls had hauled in a couple of crates of fresh fruit and vegetables, a couple of bags of rice, and a bag of salt.

"Between the seven of us, they should last about a week. More if we ration." Stepping a bit closer, she lowered her voice and asked, "How are we um… taking care of other needs. There's not exactly an outhouse."

"Over the side. Very carefully. I installed a folding seat and a grab bar. You'll be fine."

"And um, after?"

"We've got some toilet paper, but your island's general store didn't carry more for us to buy. What do you use on Kyoshi?" I asked, since we had brought a roll from the ship to use for our personal needs.

"Shells, mostly," Suki admitted. "Should I ask Toph to make some scrapers before we set out?"

I made a face, but nodded. I'd had to use a few different alternatives to paper at times and almost none of them were great, but you made do with what you had. "Yeah. Go ahead. Something is better than nothing. Going to go back to the general store and get more soap before we go."

Desalination, fresh water tanks, a bath and sink, and toilet seats weren't the only changes we'd made to the ship, however. With Toph now able to bend metal properly, things I had considered a only a possibility in the future sometime after the war were now suddenly possible, with a bit of ingenuity. For instance, cannon.

They weren't proper, gunpowder fired cannons, but those were on my list of things to make after the war—I just didn't want Ozai getting his hands on them if something happened. These were effectively swivel guns with sights and elevation for accuracy—one on the front, one on either side, and one on the back. They were powered by either Toph or myself through bending and shot stone, bullet shaped cannon rounds loaded from the rear down a rifled barrel—but since they were stone, Toph could bend them into grapeshot instead if we needed it. We had two vertical metal racks beside each cannon containing ten rounds each.

We had tested them from the ship with fairly impressive results—especially working together. If one of the Kyoshi girls was on loading duty, I could heat the stone and Toph could launch it at a pretty decent rate, roughly one every ten seconds, with most of that being time spent heating the round. Those hot rounds would explode on impact, with the potential to start fires. If we didn't heat them, then we could get about one every six seconds, but Toph and I could split up and use one each—her using earthbending to launch them, me using firebending to create small explosions to launch them.

Of course, those stones weren't just good for firing out of cannons. No, I'd made a release system to drop them overboard—over targets, from the air. We had tested that on the beach, to devastating effect. When it came time to deal with the pirate base, we would probably be using the ship to make a surprise bombing run at night to take out strategic targets and get their attention. We had a couple of slabs of stone loaded and strapped down for Toph to make more ammunition from if we needed it, but it wasn't as much as I'd like, given I had to keep weight limits in mind.

Eventually, we finished our preparations and everyone confirmed they were ready to set off. With the sun setting, I took us out to sea westward and a couple of the Kyoshi girls unrolled the balloon as we'd showed them and got everything into place. Soon enough, we were rising into the air and the girls moved around the boat, acting as spotters as they looked for any ships in the area. When night fell, Suki and I cooked us a meal and we divided the watch up. We made sure at least one person would be on watch outside at all times, keeping the ship on course and from running into a surprise mountain while patrolling up and down the deck, looking for light sources in the distance. Being able to see over the horizon from sea level and spot fires or other lights that could indicate the presence of pirates was one of the main reasons why I had agreed to keep the ship airborne overnight.

It was only a few days in before I found myself being shaken awake in the middle of the night. Cracking an eye open, I squinted in the moonlight coming in through the open cabin windows, barely making out one of the Kyoshi girls crouched over me.

Glancing down at Toph still sleeping, I sent the girl an amused look. "If you're wanting some hanky-panky, I'm pretty sure Toph is going to see how far up she can toss you overboard from and have you survive long enough for me to heal you."

"Hah. Tempting~," the girl purred, and I recognized her voice as the most openly degenerate one. "But no. Need you outside. Suki's already up and checking it out."

Nodding, I disentangled myself from Toph and pulled on my pants and robe, before slipping out of the curtain we'd hung between our bed and the rest of the cabin for at least the illusion of privacy. I paused only long enough to grab my spyglass, before I followed the girl to the front of the ship, where Suki stood looking off the side through her own spyglass. She looked up when I joined her, before pointing into the distance.

Far off to the northwest, I saw a flicker of light. Bringing up the spyglass, I hummed as I studied it, realizing it was probably a lamp given the size of it. "Adjust course north, northwest. Increase speed one third."

"Aye, aye," the Kyoshi girl hurried off and a moment later, the ship turned and began to pick up speed.

Eventually, I made out sails and the body of a ship. Suki called it out at the same time. "That's a ship."

I grinned. "Well then. Let's follow it and see where it goes. We'll ascend a bit and match our speed to his. Hang back here in his shadow and watch. I'll need to check the map, but I think he's off the normal shipping lanes."

"So, a pirate?" Suki asked, and I made a so-so gesture.

"Pirate, someone avoiding pirates in the normal shipping lanes, or a merchant working with pirates to fence goods. We'll learn more when daybreak comes."

Wandering Prince
Avatar the Last Airbender, Zuko SI
33
Commissioned by LurksTheMost.
"Alright, let's go over it again," I said, looking at the three Kyoshi girls who would be staying behind.

One of them—the bitchy one—rolled her eyes and Suki glared. "Girls."

The girls straightened up a bit and the irritable one sighed. "Three red means retreat, circle around to the east, descend over the far side of the island south of the eastern port, and prepare for combat because the mission's blown and either someone's been captured or you're coming in hot."

"Three blue means come down over the south and descend, situation normal," the horny one continued.

The last one finished, "Three green means you need immediate exfiltration. Dive, drop a rope, and fly over where we saw the flares come up from fast for pickup. Two of us will use our bows to make sure no one tries to board."

"You're forgetting one," the fourth Kyoshi girl pointed out. "Red, green, blue. Pull back, set down on the water over the horizon, then return tomorrow night."

"And a signal fire from the highest point on the island means something has happened and we need pickup from that location," Suki supplied.

"That's it," I confirmed.

"Are we ready to go yet?" Toph asked, thumping into my side with an annoyed sigh.

I looked to Suki, who nodded. "We're good."

"Alright." I looked to Toph. "Remember, don't struggle. Deep breath before you let go."

The girl nodded and we moved over to the rope hanging off the side of the ship. Suki went down first, followed by her sister. I waited until I heard the second splash, before grabbing the rope and sliding myself down. Looking up, I spotted Toph following me down and let go. The drop to the ocean was short and I was back above the surface before she was at the bottom.

As soon as she let go, I moved forward and dove after her, grabbing her before she could get too far down. With a heave, I pulled her to the surface and Toph gasped as I pulled her up against my chest, and started stroking for the shore with one hand—Suki's sister following behind us to make sure we didn't go off course. Above us, the ship pulled away, climbing higher and turning to circle around

"Nice, even kicks," I spoke into her ear and she nodded, her legs starting to kick as she matched the rhythm of my own kicking.

"I hate the ocean," she grumbled quietly as she clung on tightly to my arm under her breasts.

"Not my favorite," I admitted. "Who knows what could be down there."

"Shut up~!"

We'd tried to teach Toph how to swim and between Yue and I, we had done a fairly good job. The problem was, Toph's muscle to fat ratio meant she sank unless she actively worked to stay up. And while that was fine when we had a waterbender around to fish her out of the drink if she slipped up, and the places where we'd taught her to swim weren't too deep anyway, we didn't have Yue with us now and if she went under and I lost track of her, she'd be gone—and neither of us trusted her ability to swim well enough to chance that. But we needed her on the island, so I'd agreed to carry her in.

Eventually, I heard Suki up ahead as she hauled herself out of the water. "It should be nearly deep enough to stand in, Zuko."

I pulled a few more strokes, then reoriented and stood, hefting Toph up to her feet as we left the water, the last Kyoshi girl hurrying up behind us, laughing quietly. "That was fun!"

"Toph?" I asked as we moved up out of the waves, blasting a wave of heat off of my body to dry off and then taking a moment to do the same for the others as best I could.

"Yeah, gimme a minute," she said, visibly focusing before the rocks and sand at her feet turned into a pair of her usual sandals, with stone twisted into rope taking the place of the straps. A moment later, I felt a faint rumble in the earth beneath us, then for just a second there was a sound just at the edge of my hearing.

We gathered around as the sand in front of Toph shifted, rising up to take the shape of the island—generally arrowhead shaped, with an interior lake. The south side of the island rose at a somewhat steep angle to the top of what was obviously an old caldera before descending to the mostly flat center, and a depression in the middle with the lake. To the northwest, things tapered in the arrowhead shape, with the land much less steep down to the far side. From our observations from the air, we knew it to be roughly two miles from the northernmost tip to the southernmost, and a mile and a half wide at the widest point, directly across the caldera to the south.

Spoiler: Island Map

There were three ports—one on the northern tip of the island, one on the east side of the island, and one on the southwest. The eastern and southwestern ports were both new construction—the work of earthbenders, given that they had cut paths up the caldera and then made their own tunnels into the inner part of the island. The port to the north had looked much older from the air and seemed to be mostly made of wood—and it was where the small fleet of fishing boats belonging to the island's original inhabitants were still tied up. However, we hadn't seen any of them go out in our observation from the air the day before and we had all come to the conclusion that it was very possible that the natives had either been forcibly relocated, or more likely enslaved.

Studying the map Toph made, there appeared to be two major villages and three minor ones on the island. The smaller villages had sprung up around the ports and, even at this hour, were busy with people moving back and forth through the streets. The two larger ones were in the north near what had looked from the air like farmland, and in the caldera beside the lake, with what looked very much like a palace surrounded by a village worth of buildings and tall walls.

"That's a lot of people," Suki murmured.

"Are those… cages?" the other Kyoshi girl asked, pointing to the northern village—specifically, to the blocky shapes of buildings that were open from the top for us to see into.

"Looks that way," Toph nodded. "There are stone bars over all the windows and doors too, but they're kind of hard to show from here—"

"It's fine Toph, this is great," I told her, before pointing at the palace in the caldera and the village surrounding it. "What do you think? Looks like somewhere a leader would fort up to my eyes."

Suki hummed, before nodding. "Most likely. So then, this is their main base," she pointed to the palace village, "this is where they're holding their prisoners," the northern village, "and the other three are for taking in and sending out goods?"

"Makes sense to me, but we should confirm it," I agreed. "Split up?"

"Mm," Suki agreed. "We'll take the eastern port if you'll go west. We'll climb inland and meet south of the northern port?"

Considering the map, I nodded. "Sounds good. And if you have to drop any bodies—"

"We'll clean up after ourselves and make sure no one finds them," Suki confirmed. "If we don't see you by daylight?"

I pointed to the northwest corner of the caldera—the highest point on the island, overlooking both the interior of the caldera and the port to the north. "Head here, then signal for pickup. If we don't see you, we'll head there first and wait."

I left it unsaid, but the implication was clear—if the girls didn't show up, Toph and I would track them down and bail them out, but we didn't expect them to come for us without backup.

We split up and Toph and I hurried up the beach. Thankfully, we didn't really have to worry about leaving tracks given just how rocky the beach was. On the other hand, in the dark the terrain made it very easy to potentially misstep and twist or roll an ankle, so going was slow and much too noisy for my liking. The lack of trees or anywhere to really hide was irritating, so I did the next best thing and led us up the caldera's slope so we would at least be above any potential threat and have a better view of anyone approaching.

Soon enough, we began to hear sounds on the wind—muffled conversations and someone picking at a stringed instrument. The dock and the little town came into sight and Toph and I crouched and watched for a while in silence.

Eventually, she murmured, "Doesn't look like much. A few houses for the guys who work here, some storage buildings, and the bar." She cocked her head slightly, then amended, "Or brothel. Both I think. Everyone's in there or sleeping."

"Let's go have a look," I whispered.

"No, just normal pirates, I think."

"How are the others doing?"

"They don't look like they're rushing, or they've raised the alarm?" I asked, and she shook her head.

"Alright, we'll keep moving and you can have another look when we get where we're going."

She nodded and we continued our climb up the side of the caldera, careful not to slip on any of the moss or lichen growing on the rocky slope while staying low enough to hopefully not silhouette us against the sky if anyone from the port happened to step outside and look in our direction. It was cloudy tonight, but the moon was just shy of full, so while it was dark there was still enough light for two people moving up the slope to be spotted if we weren't careful. We passed our backup rendezvous spot, stopping only long enough to make sure it would be visible from the air before moving on.

As we got close to the northern village, we stepped off of the path and into the forest, carefully making our way around and down the slope until we reached the smaller northern port village. We took a few minutes to check the port itself and found it was practically identical to the first one, save for the fact that most of the buildings were older, original wood construction and had clearly been a fishing village before it was captured. "Great," I nodded, leaning against a tree and making myself comfortable. A moment later, Toph settled in my lap and leaned back against my chest. Toph hummed, closing her eyes and pressing her feet flat against the ground. After a moment, she shrugged. "I can feel lava beneath the surface."

"Magma." At the word, Toph shifted to send me an annoyed look. "It's magma beneath the surface and lava only once it's above the surface."

"Fine. Mag-ma," she rolled the word over her tongue and I chuckled.

She considered for a moment before nodding. "Sure, but why would I wanna? I thought we were taking this place back, not burning it down."

"We are," I confirmed. "But they've obviously got more than one earthbender working for them. I want to know how hard it would be for them to decide to blow us all up if it starts looking like they're going to lose."

"Oh," Toph murmured. Humming, she thought about it and shook her head. "The hollow below us doesn't feel like it's under much pressure. I could make it blow, but it wouldn't blow big, you know? "Suki~! You shouldn't have interrupted them! It's not polite!" her sister protested, before a grin spread over her lips. "Another minute and we'd have gotten a free show."

Suki nodded. "Four ships at the eastern port. All large. We counted at least two hundred men." Frowning, she asked, "You're sure you didn't see any benders? Because I didn't either."

"Nope. None," Toph shook her head. "Or if they were, they weren't being obvious about it."

The four of us shared a look before Suki suggested, "Do you think they're in that palace?"

Toph snorted. "Bunch of pirate benders playing at being royalty? Wouldn't doubt it."

I shook my head. "I don't know her. Uncle suspected he knew who she is from his time in the service, but he didn't tell me anything about her, other than to stay away. I can't say what she would or wouldn't do just from that. Going by the sorts of things people with power have historically done however, and the fact that she probably has the common sense to know that eventually the Fire Navy will come for her… It seems logical to me that she'd choose to fort up in the most defensible position on the island and surround herself with all of the people who can potentially ward off an attack."

The leader of the Kyoshi Warriors nodded and we stood, brushing off the twigs and leaves, before moving quietly through the forest towards the village. The trees gave way to a plain overgrown with tall pampas grass, white tips swaying in the breeze and standing as high as my chest—bare patches indicating where the local farmers had been planting their crops before the pirates arrived.

There was a brief moment of tense silence, before Suki and Toph both nodded. With that, we fell silent and pushed just a bit faster to make it to the rendezvous.

Wandering Prince
Avatar the Last Airbender, Zuko SI
34
Commissioned by LurksTheMost.

Dark clouds were rolling in from the west, bringing with them a line of rain like a wall and lightning popping all across the storm front. We had barely outrun it and just had time to set down and secure our own ship after spotting Uncle's vessel.

The older man hurried over to us as the first sprinkles of rain started to patter over the deck. "Nephew! You've returned," Uncle greeted with a smile as he looked over our group. "And you've brought friends. Come, let us get inside, before the rain comes. We can have tea."

We followed Uncle inside, and just in time as nearly as soon as we were through the hatch we heard the sound of rain and hail hammering the metal deck outside. Somewhere behind me, I heard the Kyoshi girls comment.

"That sounds nasty."

"Yeah, glad we got down before it hit. Wouldn't want to be in the air and get caught in it."

"Do you think Zuko's boat will be okay?"

"I hope. All our stuff is in there!"

"Zuko?" Suki asked, and I turned to send her a grin.

"Those ships are supposed to be able to ride out most storms on the high seas. So, assuming we don't get hundred foot swells, it should be fine. If we do, we've got bigger problems than worrying about my boat capsizing."

Beside me, Toph let out a quiet groan. "I already don't feel great. I hate the ocean."

Reaching out, I pulled her against my side and gave her a squeeze, which she eagerly returned. Ahead of us, Uncle opened a door and led us inside, to the same room we had used for tea last time. We set down the bags we'd brought over, expecting the storm to last a couple of days, and joined Uncle around the table as someone brought in a tea pot.

"Girls, this is my uncle Iroh. But everyone just calls him Uncle," I introduced as we got settled in. "And Uncle, these are—"

"The Kyoshi Warriors," Uncle chuckled, heating the water in the pot and starting the tea to steeping. "The descendants of Avatar Kyoshi's honor guard, and the women she saved. It is a pleasure to meet you all."

"You as well," Suki returned, if a bit awkwardly given she knew just who Uncle was. "You're… not what I was expecting."

Uncle laughed. "I'll take that as a compliment." Letting out a sigh, his smile fell a bit as he turned serious. "But you are not here for pleasantries. If you returned, it means you've found something."

"I recognize this island. There was nothing on it but a small fishing village. We considered it for installing a signaling station, but ultimately decided on Whale Tail Island instead," Uncle mused, stroking his beard.
